sermon:
A man named Epaphras walked a long way to bring Paul news, and the news was good. A church Paul had never visited, in a town off the main road, was holding. Faith in Christ. Love for the saints. Hope laid up in heaven. Paul, chained somewhere in Rome, hears about a congregation he has never seen, and the first thing out of his mouth is thanksgiving. Not strategy. Not anxiety over the false teaching already creeping in. Thanksgiving. That is where Colossians begins, and where it begins tells you what Paul thinks the gospel actually is.

**The gospel is a living thing**

Paul will not let the Colossians think their faith is a local product, a regional brand of religion that happened to land in their valley. He writes that the gospel "is bearing fruit and increasing—as it also does among you, since the day you heard it and understood the grace of God in truth" (Colossians 1:6). Notice the verbs. Bearing fruit. Increasing. The same word he uses of the gospel in the whole world he uses of the gospel in Colossae. It is one seed. It does the same thing everywhere because it carries the same life. The gospel is not advice that needs a culture to make it work. It is an organism that grows wherever it is planted, the way a vine does not ask permission of the soil.

This matters because a growing thing cannot be controlled the way a manufactured thing can. We want our faith manageable. We want it to behave, to stay the size we built it. But Paul describes something that came in from outside, took root, and started doing what it does—whether or not anyone was managing it. The fruit in Colossae was not the achievement of the Colossians. It was the gospel doing what the gospel does.

**The prayer is not for ease**

Then watch what Paul prays. If I were writing to a young church surrounded by error and pressure, I would pray for relief. Paul does not. He prays that they would "be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding," and the goal of that knowledge is "to walk in a manner worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him, bearing fruit in every good work" (Colossians 1:9-10). Knowledge that produces a life. Not knowledge that produces comfort, or that ends the trouble, but knowledge worked all the way down into how a person walks on a Tuesday.

I have to be honest about how foreign this prayer is to my own praying. Most of my prayers are requests for the situation to change. Paul prays for the person to be changed inside the situation. He asks God to strengthen them with all power—for what? For great deliverance? No. "For all endurance and patience with joy" (Colossians 1:11). Power to keep standing. That is a prayer for people who are not going to be rescued out of difficulty but are going to be held through it.

**He has already done the impossible part**

And then Paul names what God has already done, and it is the part no growth and no prayer could accomplish. The Father "has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins" (Colossians 1:13-14). Transferred. Past tense. The decisive move is finished. Before the Colossians bore any fruit, before they prayed any prayer, the Son had bought them out and carried them across.

This is the supremacy of Christ stated quietly, before Paul makes it thunder in the next paragraph. The whole letter is going to insist that Jesus is enough, that nothing needs adding to Him. Here is the first proof: the people doing the growing did not move themselves out of darkness. He did. The fruit grows because the soil was already conquered ground, ground He took at the cross.

So I will stop pretending the life in me is mine to take credit for, and stop pretending the dryness in me is mine to fix by effort. The gospel that came to Colossae is the gospel that came to me, and it does the same thing in both. It grows. Not because I am good ground. Because it carries its own life, and it landed.

The gospel grows where it lands.

Stand in front of something that has lasted—an old stone bridge, a cathedral that outlived the empire that built it—and you feel a question rise without words. What holds this together. What keeps it from falling. Paul takes that question and aims it at everything that exists, and then he answers it with a name. Colossae was a town drowning in spiritual options: angels to appease, powers to manage, a hierarchy of unseen beings you had to keep happy to stay safe. Into that crowded sky Paul drops a hymn that empties it. There is one who is above all of it, and through Him all of it stands.

**Above creation, before creation, holding creation**

Paul writes that Christ "is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15). Firstborn does not mean first made. It is a word of rank, of inheritance, of priority. He is not the eldest item in the list of created things. He is the heir who stands over the whole estate. Paul makes that unmistakable: "by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through him and for him" (Colossians 1:16).

Read that list again. Thrones, dominions, rulers, authorities. Those are exactly the powers the Colossians were afraid of, the beings the false teachers said you had to negotiate with. Paul does not deny they exist. He files them under "created." Every power you fear is a thing He made. And then the line that holds the universe in place: "in him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:17). Not held together once and left to run. Held together now, this second, by the active will of the Son. Take Him out and the bridge falls.

**The cross is in the same sentence as the cosmos**

Here is where the hymn turns and where most of us are not ready for it. The same Christ who made the galaxies is the Christ who bled. Paul refuses to keep the cosmic Jesus and the crucified Jesus in separate rooms. "For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile to himself all things... making peace by the blood of his cross" (Colossians 1:19-20). The one who holds the stars in place made peace by being broken. The blood of the cross is not a small chapter in a large story. It is the means by which the Maker reconciles what He made.

We like the Christ who holds things together. He is grand, and He flatters our sense that the universe is sturdy. We are slower with the Christ whose hands were opened by nails. But Paul will not let us have one without the other. The supremacy and the suffering are the same Lord. The hands that uphold all things are the hands that were pierced.

**You were on the wrong side of that peace**

And then Paul comes for me directly. Lest I admire the hymn from a safe distance, he says what I was. "And you, who once were alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds, he has now reconciled in his body of flesh by his death" (Colossians 1:21-22). Alienated. Hostile in mind. Not neutral, not merely confused—an enemy in my thinking, doing the deeds that flowed from it. That is the honest diagnosis, and I cannot soften it without lying. The reconciliation in this hymn is not God making peace with a misunderstanding. It is God making peace with His enemies, at the cost of His Son's body.

So the cosmic claim lands as a personal one. If He holds all things together, He is holding me, including the parts of me that were once set against Him. The man who was hostile in mind is held in place by the one he was hostile toward. That is the supremacy of Christ doing its deepest work—not far off among the thrones and dominions, but down inside a reconciled enemy who now belongs to Him.

There is nothing that stands apart from this Christ. Not the powers. Not the stars. Not me.

In Him all things hold together.

Paul is in chains, and he calls it joy. That sentence should stop us before we go any further. A man under arrest, his movement gone, his future uncertain, writes to a church he has never met and says, "Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake" (Colossians 1:24). We are trained to read suffering as interruption, the thing that gets in the way of the work. Paul reads his suffering as part of the work. Something is being accomplished through what is being done to him, and he wants the Colossians to know what it is.

**The mystery was always meant to come out**

Paul says he was made a minister "to make the word of God fully known, the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints" (Colossians 1:25-26). A mystery, in Paul's vocabulary, is not a riddle that keeps you guessing. It is something God kept covered until the right moment and then uncovered on purpose. For ages it was hidden. Now it is told. And Paul's whole assignment is to be one of the people doing the telling, even from a cell.

We should sit with how much of God's plan ran underground before it surfaced. Generations lived and died inside a story whose center had not yet been disclosed. Then the center was disclosed, and it turned out not to be a doctrine you could file away but a presence you could not get rid of.

**The mystery is a person, and He is in His people**

Here is the heart of it, and Paul states it in a phrase that should never become familiar enough to lose its weight. The mystery is "Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:27). The hidden thing of the ages turns out to have a name. It is not a system. It is not a secret technique for living. It is Christ Himself, dwelling in ordinary people, and that indwelling is the only ground of any real hope they have of glory.

This is the supremacy of Christ pressed all the way into the human chest. Not Christ above us only, holding the cosmos—though He does that—but Christ in us, the actual residence of God in people who, by themselves, have no claim to glory at all. The false teachers in Colossae were offering extras: visions, rules, ranks of angels, hidden knowledge for the advanced. Paul says the advanced thing, the secret thing, the thing worth everything, is already inside the simplest believer. Christ. Him. Nothing added.

**This is what Paul is sweating for**

And this is why Paul works the way he does. "For this I toil, struggling with all his energy that he powerfully works within me" (Colossians 1:29). The word for struggle is the word for an athlete's agony in the contest. He is not coasting. He is straining—so that the church would "be knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God's mystery, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:2-3). Knit together. Assured. Owning treasures they already possess in Christ but have not yet unwrapped.

I have to ask myself whether I struggle for anyone like this. Paul is in agony of effort for a congregation in a town he has never walked through. My care tends to extend as far as my convenience and stop. I will pray for people up to the point where praying costs me sleep, and then I quit. Paul's labor exposes how thin mine is, and it exposes something else: that the treasure he is laboring to hand people is one they cannot manufacture and I cannot manufacture for them. All the wisdom is hidden in Christ. The most I can do is point, and toil, and point again at the one already living in them.

So the assurance Colossae needed was not more religious machinery. It was Christ, in them, the whole treasure, already given. And the assurance I need on my worst day is the same. Not a better technique. A present Christ.

The mystery has a name.

There is a particular kind of religious person who is never finished. Always one more rule, one more experience, one more level of insight just out of reach. The teachers troubling Colossae specialized in exactly this. You have Christ, fine—but have you kept the festivals? Have you seen the visions? Have you submitted to the regulations that separate the serious from the ordinary? It is a sales pitch built on a manufactured lack, and Paul demolishes it with a single word repeated through the chapter. Filled. Complete. Full. You are not missing anything.

**Walk the way you arrived**

Paul starts with a simple instruction that turns out to govern everything: "as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith" (Colossians 2:6-7). How did you receive Him? By grace, with empty hands, trusting Him and not your performance. Then walk that way. Do not switch methods after you start. People come to Christ by faith and then try to grow by effort, by rules, by spiritual achievement, as if grace got them in the door and now they are on their own. Paul says no—the same way in is the only way forward. Rooted. The image is a tree drawing everything it needs from soil it did not make.

**The fullness is in Him, and you are in Him**

Then the great claim: "For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority" (Colossians 2:9-10). Stop and let the logic land. All the fullness of God lives in Christ. And you have been filled in Him. Not partly. Filled. If the entire fullness of God is in Christ, and you are in Christ, there is no spiritual completeness available somewhere outside Him that you are missing. The teachers were trying to sell water to people standing in the ocean.

Paul then describes what actually happened to the believer—a circumcision not made with hands, a death and burial and raising with Christ in baptism, and the cancellation of the debt: God "having canceled the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands... nailing it to the cross" (Colossians 2:14). The certificate of debt with my name on it has been nailed up where Christ was nailed. And then the powers, the very beings the Colossians feared, were disarmed: "He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him" (Colossians 2:15). The cross looked like His defeat. It was their defeat, paraded in public.

**So stop letting people grade you**

Now the application turns hard and personal. "Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ" (Colossians 2:16-17). A shadow. The rules pointed forward to Him, and now that He is here, going back to the shadow is going backward. Paul exposes the whole system: it has "an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh" (Colossians 2:23). It looks rigorous. It looks holy. It does nothing to the actual problem.

I know this temptation from the inside, and I will not pretend otherwise. Self-made religion flatters me. It lets me measure my seriousness, rank myself above the casual, feel the satisfaction of severity. And Paul calls it powerless against the very flesh it claims to discipline. The hard rules never killed my sin. They only gave my pride a uniform. The whole apparatus of looking advanced is a way of stepping out from under the head and trying to grow on my own, which Paul has already named as the one fatal move—"not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body... grows with a growth that is from God" (Colossians 2:19).

This is the supremacy of Christ as freedom. If He is the head over every power, and the fullness of God is in Him, and I am in Him, then no teacher, no rule, no experience can add a single thing to what He has already made me. The pressure to be more than complete is a lie, and I can set it down.

You are complete in Him.

Ask someone what they think about, when no one is requiring them to think about anything, and you will learn what they actually love. The mind, left alone, drifts toward what it treasures. Paul knows this, and so when he turns from doctrine to daily life in Colossians 3, he does not start with behavior. He starts with the mind. Change what you are aimed at, he says, and the rest will follow. And what he aims us at is a person who is already seated above it all.

**You are already up there with Him**

The chapter opens on a fact, not a demand: "If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God" (Colossians 3:1). The command rests on something already true. You have been raised with Christ. This is not a goal to reach but a position to live from. And Paul deepens it: "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3). Hidden. Your real life is not on display, not measured by your visible circumstances, not in danger from anything down here. It is stored where Christ is, safe in God, waiting to be revealed when He is.

So to set the mind above is not escapism. It is realism. It is thinking about where you actually are. The man whose life is hidden with Christ in God who spends all his thought on what is below is the one out of touch with reality. The upward look is the sober look.

**Kill what is already dead, wear what you already are**

Then Paul gets specific and physical. "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry" (Colossians 3:5). Put to death. Not manage, not balance, not moderate—kill. And notice he ends the list with covetousness and calls it idolatry, which means the sins of the body and the sins of the heart are the same crime: putting something below in the place that belongs to Christ above. He adds the sins we excuse because they hide in speech and temper—anger, wrath, malice, slander, lying. The respectable sins make the list right next to the scandalous ones.

And then he says to dress: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and... forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive" (Colossians 3:12-13). The standard of my forgiving is the measure of His forgiving me. That is a steep wall, and I will not pretend I scale it easily. The person I am slowest to forgive has wronged me less than I have wronged God, and I know it, and I still hold the grudge. Paul does not let me keep the old clothes because they are comfortable. He says I have already died to them. Take them off.

**Let Him rule the room and dwell in the house**

How does any of this happen without becoming the self-made religion Paul just demolished in chapter 2? The difference is the center. "Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts... And let the word of Christ dwell in you richly" (Colossians 3:15-16). Rule and dwell—let Him govern, let His word move in and take up residence. This is not effort apart from Him. It is making room for Him. And the climax names why the old categories collapse: in this new self "Christ is all, and in all" (Colossians 3:11). All. The supremacy of Christ has come home from the cosmos into the conduct, and the same Lord who holds the universe together now holds together a forgiven, re-clothed, upward-looking life.

Paul ends the section with a rule that covers everything left over: "whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him" (Colossians 3:17). Nothing is too small to be done in His name. Nothing is so ordinary it falls outside His lordship.

So I examine where my mind goes when it is free, and I am not always proud of the answer. But the cure is not to scold my mind into better thoughts. It is to remember where I am seated, and look there.

Set your mind above.

Most letters that climb as high as Colossians does—the image of the invisible God, the fullness of deity, all things holding together in Christ—would not know how to come back down. Paul does. He takes the cosmic Christ who holds the galaxies and walks Him straight into a kitchen, a workplace, a marriage, a list of names. The test of whether you believe in the supremacy of Christ is not whether you can sing the hymn of chapter 1. It is whether He is Lord of how you treat the people you live with on Thursday.

**Lordship comes home**

Paul addresses wives, husbands, children, fathers, and then at length, slaves and masters—the ordinary structures of a first-century household. And through every instruction runs one phrase that changes everything: as to the Lord. Wives submit "as is fitting in the Lord." Children obey, "for this pleases the Lord." And to those with the least power and most reason to work only when watched, he says, "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ" (Colossians 3:23-24).

This is the supremacy of Christ pressed into labor that no one applauds. The work done where no human boss can see it is done in full view of the Lord who upholds all things. That dignifies the unseen worker and it indicts the lazy one, and Paul means both. He even warns the masters that they have a Master in heaven—the powerful are not exempt from the lordship that protects the weak.

**Pray like the outcome depends on it, watch like it does**

Then Paul turns to prayer, and he refuses to let it become routine. "Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving" (Colossians 4:2). Steadfastly—the word means to keep at it, to refuse to quit. Watchful—alert, not drowsy, not going through motions. And even here Paul, the apostle who has just been preaching the all-sufficiency of Christ, asks them to pray for him: that God would "open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison" (Colossians 4:3). He does not ask first for his chains to fall off. He asks for an open door for the message. The man in prison wants the gospel free more than he wants himself free.

And toward outsiders he asks for a life that matches the message: "Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt" (Colossians 4:5-6). Gracious and salted—warm and with an edge, kind without being bland. I have to weigh my own speech toward the people watching from outside the faith, and I find it is often neither. Sour when it should be gracious, or limp when it should have salt. Paul will not let witness be careless.

**The gospel rides on real shoulders**

And then the names. Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark, Justus, Epaphras who is always struggling in prayer for them, Luke the beloved physician, Demas, Nympha and the church in her house, Archippus. Verse after verse of ordinary people. It would be easy to skip this part as a postscript. Do not. After two chapters establishing that Christ is supreme over every power in the universe, Paul grounds the whole letter in a list of coworkers who actually carried the gospel from town to town on real feet. The cosmic Lord advances His kingdom through Tychicus delivering a letter and Epaphras agonizing in prayer.

That is the honest shape of it, and it implicates me. I would rather admire the supremacy of Christ in the abstract than render it in the dishes, the day job, the steady prayer, the gracious word, the unglamorous labor of being one more name on the list of people who carried something for someone else. Paul leaves no room for a Christ who is Lord of the cosmos but not of my Monday. The same Jesus holds both.

Whatever you do, do it for Him.
